name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_SYSTEMS_OF_PARTICLES_AND_ROTATIONAL_MOTION_MCQ_Q01 - Definition of an ideal rigid body

questiontext.text: Which of the following statements correctly defines an ideal rigid body in physics?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In classical mechanics, an extended body is modeled as an assembly or system of microscopic particles.

Step 2: Distance Invariance Condition
Ideally, a rigid body is defined as a body having a perfectly definite and unchanging shape, such that the distances between all pairs of particles composing the body do not change under any applied forces.

Step 3: Comparison with Real Bodies
Real bodies deform to some extent under external forces, but when such deformations are negligible, they are idealized as rigid bodies.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The defining characteristic of an ideal rigid body is that the inter-particle separations remain constant at all times.

Final Answer: A body with a perfectly definite and unchanging shape in which the distances between all pairs of particles do not change.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_SYSTEMS_OF_PARTICLES_AND_ROTATIONAL_MOTION_MCQ_Q02 - Velocity of particles in pure translational motion

questiontext.text: In pure translational motion of a rigid body at any given instant of time:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Pure translational motion of a rigid body is defined as motion where every line segment connecting any two particles of the body remains parallel to its initial direction throughout.

Step 2: Displacement Analysis
Since the relative orientation and distances between particles remain fixed, the displacement vectors of all particles during any given time interval \(\Delta t\) are identical: \(\Delta \mathbf{r}_1 = \Delta \mathbf{r}_2 = \dots = \Delta \mathbf{r}_n\).

Step 3: Instantaneous Velocity
Differentiating displacement with respect to time yields \(\mathbf{v}_1 = \mathbf{v}_2 = \dots = \mathbf{v}_n = \mathbf{V}_{\text{cm}}\).

Step 4: Final Conclusion
At any instant of time, all particles in a body undergoing pure translational motion possess identical linear velocities.

Final Answer: all particles of the rigid body have the same velocity.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_SYSTEMS_OF_PARTICLES_AND_ROTATIONAL_MOTION_MCQ_Q03 - Center of mass of two equal masses

questiontext.text: Two particles of equal mass \(m\) are situated along the \(x\)-axis at positions \(x_1 = 4\text{ m}\) and \(x_2 = 12\text{ m}\). What is the position coordinate \(X\) of the center of mass of the system?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Masses: \(m_1 = m\), \(m_2 = m\). Positions: \(x_1 = 4\text{ m}\), \(x_2 = 12\text{ m}\).

Step 2: Relevant Formula
The center of mass position for a two-particle system along the \(x\)-axis is given by:
\[X = \frac{m_1 x_1 + m_2 x_2}{m_1 + m_2}\]

Step 3: Step-by-Step Calculation
Substitute the given values into the formula:
\[X = \frac{m(4\text{ m}) + m(12\text{ m})}{m + m} = \frac{m(4 + 12)}{2m} = \frac{16}{2}\text{ m} = 8\text{ m}\]

Step 4: Verification
For two equal masses, the center of mass lies exactly midway between them: \(\frac{4 + 12}{2} = 8\text{ m}\).

Final Answer: \(8\text{ m}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_SYSTEMS_OF_PARTICLES_AND_ROTATIONAL_MOTION_MCQ_Q04 - Center of mass of a homogeneous circular ring

questiontext.text: On the basis of reflection symmetry, the center of mass of a homogeneous, uniform thin circular ring:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
For a homogeneous body of regular shape, the distribution of mass exhibits geometric reflection symmetry about its geometric center.

Step 2: Integral Formulation
Choosing the geometric center as the origin, for every mass element \(\mathrm{d}m\) located at coordinate vector \(\mathbf{r}\), there exists a symmetric element of equal mass \(\mathrm{d}m\) at \(-\mathbf{r}\).

Step 3: Vanishing of Integral
The sum and hence the integral \(\int \mathbf{r}\,\mathrm{d}m = \mathbf{0}\), which establishes that the center of mass coincides with the geometric center.

Step 4: Location Check
Because the mass of a thin circular ring is distributed entirely along its circumference, the geometric center lies in empty space outside the material of the ring.

Final Answer: lies at its geometric center, which is located outside the material of the ring.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_SYSTEMS_OF_PARTICLES_AND_ROTATIONAL_MOTION_MCQ_Q05 - Cross product of a vector with itself

questiontext.text: For any arbitrary non-zero vector \(\mathbf{a}\), the vector product \(\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{a}\) is equal to:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Definition of Vector Product
The vector product of two vectors \(\mathbf{a}\) and \(\mathbf{b}\) is defined as \(\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b} = (ab\sin\theta)\hat{\mathbf{n}}\), where \(\theta\) is the angle between them and \(\hat{\mathbf{n}}\) is a unit vector perpendicular to their plane.

Step 2: Angle Evaluation
When a vector is crossed with itself, \(\mathbf{b} = \mathbf{a}\), so the angle between the two vectors is \(\theta = 0^\circ\).

Step 3: Magnitude Evaluation
The magnitude of the cross product is \(|\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{a}| = a^2 \sin 0^\circ = 0\).

Step 4: Final Conclusion
A vector with zero magnitude is defined as the null vector \(\mathbf{0}\).

Final Answer: a null vector \(\mathbf{0}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_SYSTEMS_OF_PARTICLES_AND_ROTATIONAL_MOTION_MCQ_Q06 - Cyclic cross product of Cartesian unit vectors

questiontext.text: In a standard right-handed Cartesian coordinate system, which of the following vector cross products is correct?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In a right-handed orthogonal triad, the Cartesian unit vectors \(\hat{\mathbf{i}}, \hat{\mathbf{j}}, \hat{\mathbf{k}}\) satisfy cyclic cross product rules.

Step 2: Right-Hand Screw Rule
Turning from \(\hat{\mathbf{j}}\) to \(\hat{\mathbf{k}}\) advances the screw along the positive \(x\)-axis, yielding \(\hat{\mathbf{j}} \times \hat{\mathbf{k}} = \hat{\mathbf{i}}\).

Step 3: Anti-Commutativity Check
Reversing the cyclic order produces negative signs: \(\hat{\mathbf{i}} \times \hat{\mathbf{j}} = \hat{\mathbf{k}}\), \(\hat{\mathbf{k}} \times \hat{\mathbf{i}} = \hat{\mathbf{j}}\), and \(\hat{\mathbf{j}} \times \hat{\mathbf{i}} = -\hat{\mathbf{k}}\).

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The relation \(\hat{\mathbf{j}} \times \hat{\mathbf{k}} = \hat{\mathbf{i}}\) is correct.

Final Answer: \(\hat{\mathbf{j}} \times \hat{\mathbf{k}} = \hat{\mathbf{i}}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_SYSTEMS_OF_PARTICLES_AND_ROTATIONAL_MOTION_MCQ_Q07 - Relation between linear speed and angular speed

questiontext.text: A rigid body rotates about a fixed axis with angular velocity \(\omega\). For a particle situated at a perpendicular distance \(r_\perp\) from the axis of rotation, the magnitude of its linear velocity \(v\) is given by:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Kinematic Principle
Every particle of a rigid body rotating about a fixed axis executes circular motion in a plane perpendicular to the axis.

Step 2: Geometry of Motion
The radius of the circular path is the perpendicular distance \(r_\perp\) of the particle from the rotation axis.

Step 3: Relation Derivation
The arc distance moved in time \(\mathrm{d}t\) is \(\mathrm{d}s = r_\perp \mathrm{d}\theta\). Dividing by \(\mathrm{d}t\) gives \(v = \frac{\mathrm{d}s}{\mathrm{d}t} = r_\perp \frac{\mathrm{d}\theta}{\mathrm{d}t} = \omega r_\perp\).

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The linear speed of the particle is \(v = \omega r_\perp\).

Final Answer: \(v = \omega r_\perp\)

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_SYSTEMS_OF_PARTICLES_AND_ROTATIONAL_MOTION_MCQ_Q08 - Dimensions and SI unit of moment of force

questiontext.text: What are the dimensional formula and the SI unit of moment of force (torque)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Formula Definition
Torque is defined as the vector product of position vector and force: \(\boldsymbol{\tau} = \mathbf{r} \times \mathbf{F}\).

Step 2: Dimensional Analysis
The dimensions of \(\mathbf{r}\) are \([\text{L}]\) and the dimensions of \(\mathbf{F}\) are \([\text{M}\text{L}\text{T}^{-2}]\). Thus, the dimensions of torque are \([\text{L}] \times [\text{M}\text{L}\text{T}^{-2}] = [\text{M}\text{L}^2\text{T}^{-2}]\).

Step 3: Unit Determination
In SI units, distance is measured in metres (\(\text{m}\)) and force in newtons (\(\text{N}\)). Therefore, the SI unit of torque is newton metre (\(\text{N}\cdot\text{m}\)).

Step 4: Final Conclusion
Torque has dimensions \([\text{M}\text{L}^2\text{T}^{-2}]\) and SI unit \(\text{N}\cdot\text{m}\).

Final Answer: \([\text{M}\text{L}^2\text{T}^{-2}]\) and \(\text{N}\cdot\text{m}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_SYSTEMS_OF_PARTICLES_AND_ROTATIONAL_MOTION_MCQ_Q09 - Condition for translational equilibrium of a rigid body

questiontext.text: A rigid body is in translational equilibrium if and only if:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Governing Principle
Newton's second law for a system of particles states that \(\frac{\mathrm{d}\mathbf{P}}{\mathrm{d}t} = \mathbf{F}_{\text{ext}}\), where \(\mathbf{P}\) is total linear momentum.

Step 2: Translational Equilibrium Definition
Translational equilibrium requires that the total linear momentum does not vary with time, meaning \(\frac{\mathrm{d}\mathbf{P}}{\mathrm{d}t} = \mathbf{0}\).

Step 3: Equilibrium Condition
This directly implies that the vector sum of all external forces acting on the rigid body must be zero: \(\sum_{i=1}^n \mathbf{F}_i = \mathbf{0}\).

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The necessary and sufficient condition for translational equilibrium is that the vector sum of all external forces acting on the body is zero.

Final Answer: the vector sum of all external forces acting on it is zero.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_SYSTEMS_OF_PARTICLES_AND_ROTATIONAL_MOTION_MCQ_Q10 - Rotational analogue of mass in linear motion

questiontext.text: In the rotational dynamics of a rigid body about a fixed axis, which physical quantity is the direct analogue of mass in translational motion?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Translational Formulation
In translational motion, mass \(M\) represents inertia, appearing in kinetic energy as \(K = \frac{1}{2} M v^2\) and in Newton's second law as \(F = M a\).

Step 2: Rotational Formulation
In rotational motion about a fixed axis, rotational kinetic energy is \(K = \frac{1}{2} I \omega^2\) and rotational dynamics is governed by \(\tau = I \alpha\).

Step 3: Comparison
Comparing \(v \leftrightarrow \omega\) and \(a \leftrightarrow \alpha\), the parameter \(I\) (moment of inertia) corresponds directly to mass \(M\).

Step 4: Final Conclusion
Moment of inertia is the rotational analogue of mass in linear motion.

Final Answer: moment of inertia.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_SYSTEMS_OF_PARTICLES_AND_ROTATIONAL_MOTION_MCQ_Q11 - Center of mass of three particles on an equilateral triangle

questiontext.text: Three particles of masses \(100\text{ g}\), \(150\text{ g}\), and \(200\text{ g}\) are located at the vertices \(O(0, 0)\), \(A(0.5\text{ m}, 0)\), and \(B(0.25\text{ m}, 0.25\sqrt{3}\text{ m})\) of an equilateral triangle of side \(0.5\text{ m}\). What are the coordinates \((X, Y)\) of the center of mass of the system?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Masses: \(m_1 = 100\text{ g}\), \(m_2 = 150\text{ g}\), \(m_3 = 200\text{ g}\). Total mass: \(M = 100 + 150 + 200 = 450\text{ g}\). Coordinates: \((x_1, y_1) = (0, 0)\), \((x_2, y_2) = (0.5, 0)\), \((x_3, y_3) = (0.25, 0.25\sqrt{3})\).

Step 2: Relevant Formulae
\[X = \frac{m_1 x_1 + m_2 x_2 + m_3 x_3}{m_1 + m_2 + m_3}, \quad Y = \frac{m_1 y_1 + m_2 y_2 + m_3 y_3}{m_1 + m_2 + m_3}\]

Step 3: Calculation of X-Coordinate
\[X = \frac{100(0) + 150(0.5) + 200(0.25)}{450} = \frac{75 + 50}{450} = \frac{125}{450} = \frac{5}{18}\text{ m}\]

Step 4: Calculation of Y-Coordinate
\[Y = \frac{100(0) + 150(0) + 200(0.25\sqrt{3})}{450} = \frac{50\sqrt{3}}{450} = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{9} = \frac{1}{3\sqrt{3}}\text{ m}\]

Step 5: Final Check
Both coordinates are positive and lie inside the triangular boundary. The center of mass is \(\left(\frac{5}{18}\text{ m}, \frac{1}{3\sqrt{3}}\text{ m}\right)\).

Final Answer: \(\left(\frac{5}{18}\text{ m}, \frac{1}{3\sqrt{3}}\text{ m}\right)\)

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_SYSTEMS_OF_PARTICLES_AND_ROTATIONAL_MOTION_MCQ_Q12 - Center of mass of uniform L shaped lamina

questiontext.text: A uniform L-shaped thin flat plate of mass \(3\text{ kg}\) is formed by three identical squares of side \(1\text{ m}\), with their centers of mass located at \(C_1(0.5\text{ m}, 0.5\text{ m})\), \(C_2(1.5\text{ m}, 0.5\text{ m})\), and \(C_3(0.5\text{ m}, 1.5\text{ m})\). What are the coordinates \((X, Y)\) of the center of mass of the lamina?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Because the lamina is uniform, each of the three squares has mass \(m_1 = m_2 = m_3 = 1\text{ kg}\). Total mass \(M = 3\text{ kg}\). Coordinates of the centers: \(C_1 = (1/2, 1/2)\), \(C_2 = (3/2, 1/2)\), \(C_3 = (1/2, 3/2)\).

Step 2: Relevant Formulae
\[X = \frac{m_1 x_1 + m_2 x_2 + m_3 x_3}{m_1 + m_2 + m_3}, \quad Y = \frac{m_1 y_1 + m_2 y_2 + m_3 y_3}{m_1 + m_2 + m_3}\]

Step 3: Calculation of X-Coordinate
\[X = \frac{1(1/2) + 1(3/2) + 1(1/2)}{1 + 1 + 1} = \frac{5/2}{3} = \frac{5}{6}\text{ m}\]

Step 4: Calculation of Y-Coordinate
\[Y = \frac{1(1/2) + 1(1/2) + 1(3/2)}{1 + 1 + 1} = \frac{5/2}{3} = \frac{5}{6}\text{ m}\]

Step 5: Symmetry Verification
By reflection symmetry across the line \(y = x\), \(X = Y\). The center of mass is at \(\left(\frac{5}{6}\text{ m}, \frac{5}{6}\text{ m}\right)\).

Final Answer: \(\left(\frac{5}{6}\text{ m}, \frac{5}{6}\text{ m}\right)\)

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_SYSTEMS_OF_PARTICLES_AND_ROTATIONAL_MOTION_MCQ_Q13 - Location of center of mass in hydrogen chloride molecule

questiontext.text: In a hydrogen chloride (\(\text{HCl}\)) molecule, the separation between the nuclei of the hydrogen and chlorine atoms is approximately \(1.27\text{ \AA}\). Given that a chlorine atom is \(35.5\) times as massive as a hydrogen atom, what is the approximate distance of the center of mass of the molecule from the hydrogen nucleus?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Coordinates
Let the hydrogen nucleus be at the origin \(x_{\text{H}} = 0\) with mass \(m_{\text{H}} = m\). The chlorine nucleus is at \(x_{\text{Cl}} = 1.27\text{ \AA}\) with mass \(m_{\text{Cl}} = 35.5m\).

Step 2: Center of Mass Formula
The position of the center of mass from the origin is given by:
\[X = \frac{m_{\text{H}} x_{\text{H}} + m_{\text{Cl}} x_{\text{Cl}}}{m_{\text{H}} + m_{\text{Cl}}}\]

Step 3: Step-by-Step Calculation
Substitute the given values:
\[X = \frac{m(0) + (35.5m)(1.27\text{ \AA})}{m + 35.5m} = \frac{35.5 \times 1.27}{36.5}\text{ \AA}\]
Computing the numerator: \(35.5 \times 1.27 = 45.085\).
Dividing by \(36.5\): \[X = \frac{45.085}{36.5} \approx 1.2352\text{ \AA} \approx 1.24\text{ \AA}\]

Step 4: Plausibility Check
Since the chlorine atom is far more massive than the hydrogen atom, the center of mass lies extremely close to the chlorine nucleus (at \(1.27 - 1.24 = 0.03\text{ \AA}\) from chlorine).

Final Answer: \(1.24\text{ \AA}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_SYSTEMS_OF_PARTICLES_AND_ROTATIONAL_MOTION_MCQ_Q14 - Acceleration of center of mass under external forces

questiontext.text: Two particles of masses \(2\text{ kg}\) and \(3\text{ kg}\) are acted upon by external forces \(\mathbf{F}_1 = 10\hat{\mathbf{i}}\text{ N}\) and \(\mathbf{F}_2 = 5\hat{\mathbf{i}} + 15\hat{\mathbf{j}}\text{ N}\) respectively. If they also exert an internal mutual gravitational attraction of \(2\text{ N}\) on each other, what is the magnitude of the acceleration of the center of mass of the system?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Masses: \(m_1 = 2\text{ kg}\), \(m_2 = 3\text{ kg}\). Total mass \(M = 2 + 3 = 5\text{ kg}\). External forces: \(\mathbf{F}_1 = 10\hat{\mathbf{i}}\text{ N}\), \(\mathbf{F}_2 = (5\hat{\mathbf{i}} + 15\hat{\mathbf{j}})\text{ N}\). Mutual internal force: \(2\text{ N}\).

Step 2: Relevant Principles
Newton's third law guarantees that internal action-reaction pairs between particles sum vectorially to zero: \(\sum \mathbf{F}_{\text{int}} = \mathbf{0}\). The acceleration of the center of mass depends exclusively on external forces:
\[M \mathbf{A}_{\text{cm}} = \mathbf{F}_{\text{ext}}\]

Step 3: Vector Sum of External Forces
\[\mathbf{F}_{\text{ext}} = \mathbf{F}_1 + \mathbf{F}_2 = (10\hat{\mathbf{i}}) + (5\hat{\mathbf{i}} + 15\hat{\mathbf{j}}) = 15\hat{\mathbf{i}} + 15\hat{\mathbf{j}}\text{ N}\]

Step 4: Calculation of Acceleration Vector
\[\mathbf{A}_{\text{cm}} = \frac{\mathbf{F}_{\text{ext}}}{M} = \frac{15\hat{\mathbf{i}} + 15\hat{\mathbf{j}}}{5} = 3\hat{\mathbf{i}} + 3\hat{\mathbf{j}}\text{ m/s}^2\]

Step 5: Magnitude Calculation
\[|\mathbf{A}_{\text{cm}}| = \sqrt{3^2 + 3^2} = \sqrt{18} = 3\sqrt{2}\text{ m/s}^2\]

Final Answer: \(3\sqrt{2}\text{ m/s}^2\)

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_SYSTEMS_OF_PARTICLES_AND_ROTATIONAL_MOTION_MCQ_Q15 - Path of center of mass of exploding projectile

questiontext.text: A projectile following a standard parabolic trajectory under uniform gravity explodes into several fragments midway in air. Assuming air resistance is negligible, the center of mass of the fragments:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The motion of the center of mass of a system of particles is governed strictly by the net external force acting on the system: \(M \mathbf{A}_{\text{cm}} = \mathbf{F}_{\text{ext}}\).

Step 2: Force Analysis During Explosion
The explosive forces that blast the projectile into fragments are purely internal forces that occur in equal and opposite pairs and sum to zero.

Step 3: External Force Evaluation
The only external force acting on the system both before and after the explosion is the uniform force of gravity, \(\mathbf{F}_{\text{ext}} = M\mathbf{g}\).

Step 4: Final Conclusion
Because the net external force and total mass remain unaltered, the acceleration of the center of mass is unchanged (\(\mathbf{g}\) downwards), and its center of mass continues precisely along the same original parabolic path.

Final Answer: continues along the same parabolic trajectory as the original projectile.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_SYSTEMS_OF_PARTICLES_AND_ROTATIONAL_MOTION_MCQ_Q16 - Motion of center of mass on a moving trolley

questiontext.text: A child sits stationary at one end of a long trolley moving uniformly with a constant speed \(V\) on a smooth, frictionless horizontal floor. If the child gets up and runs about on the trolley in any arbitrary manner, what is the speed of the center of mass of the (trolley + child) system?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: System Definition and External Forces
Consider the (child + trolley) as the system. The horizontal floor is frictionless, so the net external force acting on the system in the horizontal direction is zero: \(F_{\text{ext}, x} = 0\).

Step 2: Internal Forces
The forces exerted between the child's feet and the trolley surface are internal forces of interaction, which cancel in equal and opposite pairs.

Step 3: Conservation of Linear Momentum
According to Newton's second law for a system of particles, when \(\mathbf{F}_{\text{ext}} = \mathbf{0}\), the total linear momentum \(\mathbf{P} = M \mathbf{V}_{\text{cm}}\) remains constant.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
Since the initial horizontal speed of the center of mass was \(V\), it remains completely unaffected and equal to \(V\) regardless of the child's internal movements.

Final Answer: It remains equal to \(V\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_SYSTEMS_OF_PARTICLES_AND_ROTATIONAL_MOTION_MCQ_Q17 - Behavior of vector product under space reflection

questiontext.text: Under space reflection (parity inversion), all coordinates invert as \(x \to -x\), \(y \to -y\), and \(z \to -z\), which causes any polar vector to change sign as \(\mathbf{a} \to -\mathbf{a}\) and \(\mathbf{b} \to -\mathbf{b}\). Under this reflection, the vector product \(\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b}\):

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Definition and Transformation Rules
Under space reflection, the sign of each spatial component reverses, transforming polar vectors \(\mathbf{a}\) and \(\mathbf{b}\) into \(-\mathbf{a}\) and \(-\mathbf{b}\) respectively.

Step 2: Substitution into Vector Product
Substituting the reflected vectors into the vector product definition gives:
\[(-\mathbf{a}) \times (-\mathbf{b}) = (-1)(-1) (\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b}) = \mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b}\]

Step 3: Physical Meaning
Because \(\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b}\) does not change sign under coordinate reflection, it is classified mathematically as an axial vector (pseudovector).

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The cross product \(\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b}\) remains unchanged under space reflection.

Final Answer: remains unchanged, i.e., \(\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b} \to \mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_SYSTEMS_OF_PARTICLES_AND_ROTATIONAL_MOTION_MCQ_Q18 - Vector product of two three-dimensional vectors

questiontext.text: Two vectors are given by \(\mathbf{a} = 3\hat{\mathbf{i}} - 4\hat{\mathbf{j}} + 5\hat{\mathbf{k}}\) and \(\mathbf{b} = -2\hat{\mathbf{i}} + \hat{\mathbf{j}} - 3\hat{\mathbf{k}}\). What is the cross product \(\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b}\)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Vectors
\(\mathbf{a} = 3\hat{\mathbf{i}} - 4\hat{\mathbf{j}} + 5\hat{\mathbf{k}}\) and \(\mathbf{b} = -2\hat{\mathbf{i}} + \hat{\mathbf{j}} - 3\hat{\mathbf{k}}\).

Step 2: Determinant Formula
\[\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b} = \begin{vmatrix} \hat{\mathbf{i}} & \hat{\mathbf{j}} & \hat{\mathbf{k}} \\ a_x & a_y & a_z \\ b_x & b_y & b_z \end{vmatrix} = \begin{vmatrix} \hat{\mathbf{i}} & \hat{\mathbf{j}} & \hat{\mathbf{k}} \\ 3 & -4 & 5 \\ -2 & 1 & -3 \end{vmatrix}\]

Step 3: Expansion by Minors
\[\hat{\mathbf{i}}[(-4)(-3) - (5)(1)] - \hat{\mathbf{j}}[(3)(-3) - (5)(-2)] + \hat{\mathbf{k}}[(3)(1) - (-4)(-2)]\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Arithmetic
\[\hat{\mathbf{i}}[12 - 5] - \hat{\mathbf{j}}[-9 - (-10)] + \hat{\mathbf{k}}[3 - 8] = 7\hat{\mathbf{i}} - \hat{\mathbf{j}}(1) - 5\hat{\mathbf{k}} = 7\hat{\mathbf{i}} - \hat{\mathbf{j}} - 5\hat{\mathbf{k}}\]

Step 5: Verification
Check orthogonality: \(\mathbf{a} \cdot (\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b}) = 3(7) + (-4)(-1) + 5(-5) = 21 + 4 - 25 = 0\). The result is \(7\hat{\mathbf{i}} - \hat{\mathbf{j}} - 5\hat{\mathbf{k}}\).

Final Answer: \(7\hat{\mathbf{i}} - \hat{\mathbf{j}} - 5\hat{\mathbf{k}}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_SYSTEMS_OF_PARTICLES_AND_ROTATIONAL_MOTION_MCQ_Q19 - Direction of angular velocity vector in fixed axis rotation

questiontext.text: For a rigid body rotating about a fixed axis, the angular velocity vector \(\boldsymbol{\omega}\):

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Vector Nature of Angular Velocity
Although angular velocity can be treated algebraically as a scalar in one dimension, it is physically a vector quantity.

Step 2: Axis Orientation
For rotation about a fixed axis, every point of the rigid body revolves in a plane perpendicular to the axis of rotation.

Step 3: Direction Specification
The direction of the angular velocity vector \(\boldsymbol{\omega}\) lies along the fixed axis of rotation itself, pointing in the direction in which a right-handed screw would advance if rotated with the body.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The angular velocity vector lies along the fixed axis of rotation in accordance with the right-handed screw rule.

Final Answer: lies along the fixed axis of rotation pointing in the direction of advance of a right-handed screw turned with the rotation.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_SYSTEMS_OF_PARTICLES_AND_ROTATIONAL_MOTION_MCQ_Q20 - Calculating linear velocity from angular velocity and position vector

questiontext.text: A rigid body rotates with an angular velocity \(\boldsymbol{\omega} = 3\hat{\mathbf{i}} - 4\hat{\mathbf{j}} + \hat{\mathbf{k}}\text{ rad/s}\). What is the linear velocity of a particle of the body located at position vector \(\mathbf{r} = 5\hat{\mathbf{i}} - 6\hat{\mathbf{j}} + 6\hat{\mathbf{k}}\text{ m}\) relative to an origin on the axis of rotation?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Vectors
\(\boldsymbol{\omega} = 3\hat{\mathbf{i}} - 4\hat{\mathbf{j}} + \hat{\mathbf{k}}\text{ rad/s}\) and \(\mathbf{r} = 5\hat{\mathbf{i}} - 6\hat{\mathbf{j}} + 6\hat{\mathbf{k}}\text{ m}\).

Step 2: Relevant Formula
The linear velocity is given by the vector product: \(\mathbf{v} = \boldsymbol{\omega} \times \mathbf{r}\).

Step 3: Determinant Setup
\[\mathbf{v} = \begin{vmatrix} \hat{\mathbf{i}} & \hat{\mathbf{j}} & \hat{\mathbf{k}} \\ 3 & -4 & 1 \\ 5 & -6 & 6 \end{vmatrix}\]

Step 4: Component Expansion
\[\mathbf{v} = \hat{\mathbf{i}}[(-4)(6) - (1)(-6)] - \hat{\mathbf{j}}[(3)(6) - (1)(5)] + \hat{\mathbf{k}}[(3)(-6) - (-4)(5)]\]
\[= \hat{\mathbf{i}}[-24 + 6] - \hat{\mathbf{j}}[18 - 5] + \hat{\mathbf{k}}[-18 + 20] = -18\hat{\mathbf{i}} - 13\hat{\mathbf{j}} + 2\hat{\mathbf{k}}\text{ m/s}\]

Step 5: Orthogonality Check
\(\boldsymbol{\omega} \cdot \mathbf{v} = 3(-18) + (-4)(-13) + 1(2) = -54 + 52 + 2 = 0\). The velocity is \(-18\hat{\mathbf{i}} - 13\hat{\mathbf{j}} + 2\hat{\mathbf{k}}\text{ m/s}\).

Final Answer: \(-18\hat{\mathbf{i}} - 13\hat{\mathbf{j}} + 2\hat{\mathbf{k}}\text{ m/s}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_SYSTEMS_OF_PARTICLES_AND_ROTATIONAL_MOTION_MCQ_Q21 - Torque of a force about the origin

questiontext.text: A force \(\mathbf{F} = 7\hat{\mathbf{i}} + 3\hat{\mathbf{j}} - 5\hat{\mathbf{k}}\text{ N}\) acts on a particle whose position vector with respect to the origin is \(\mathbf{r} = \hat{\mathbf{i}} - \hat{\mathbf{j}} + \hat{\mathbf{k}}\text{ m}\). What is the torque of the force about the origin?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data
Position vector: \(\mathbf{r} = \hat{\mathbf{i}} - \hat{\mathbf{j}} + \hat{\mathbf{k}}\text{ m}\). Force: \(\mathbf{F} = 7\hat{\mathbf{i}} + 3\hat{\mathbf{j}} - 5\hat{\mathbf{k}}\text{ N}\).

Step 2: Relevant Formula
The torque about the origin is \(\boldsymbol{\tau} = \mathbf{r} \\times \mathbf{F}\).

Step 3: Determinant Representation
\[\boldsymbol{\tau} = \begin{vmatrix} \hat{\mathbf{i}} & \hat{\mathbf{j}} & \hat{\mathbf{k}} \\ 1 & -1 & 1 \\ 7 & 3 & -5 \end{vmatrix}\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Expansion
\[\boldsymbol{\tau} = \hat{\mathbf{i}}[(-1)(-5) - (1)(3)] - \hat{\mathbf{j}}[(1)(-5) - (1)(7)] + \hat{\mathbf{k}}[(1)(3) - (-1)(7)]\]
\[= \hat{\mathbf{i}}[5 - 3] - \hat{\mathbf{j}}[-5 - 7] + \hat{\mathbf{k}}[3 + 7] = 2\hat{\mathbf{i}} + 12\hat{\mathbf{j}} + 10\hat{\mathbf{k}}\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}\]

Step 5: Final Check
Verify orthogonality: \(\mathbf{r} \cdot \boldsymbol{\tau} = 1(2) + (-1)(12) + 1(10) = 2 - 12 + 10 = 0\).

Final Answer: \(2\hat{\mathbf{i}} + 12\hat{\mathbf{j}} + 10\hat{\mathbf{k}}\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_SYSTEMS_OF_PARTICLES_AND_ROTATIONAL_MOTION_MCQ_Q22 - Angular momentum of particle moving with constant velocity

questiontext.text: A single particle of mass \(m\) moves along a straight line with a constant velocity \(\mathbf{v}\). What can be asserted about its angular momentum \(\mathbf{l}\) about any chosen fixed point in space?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Formula Definition
The angular momentum of a particle of mass \(m\) moving with velocity \(\mathbf{v}\) at position \(\mathbf{r}\) about an origin is defined as \(\mathbf{l} = \mathbf{r} \times \mathbf{p} = \mathbf{r} \times (m\mathbf{v})\).

Step 2: Magnitude Evaluation
The magnitude of the angular momentum is \(l = m v (r \sin\theta)\), where \(\theta\) is the angle between \(\mathbf{r}\) and \(\mathbf{v}\).

Step 3: Geometric Invariance
The quantity \(r \sin\theta = r_\perp\) represents the perpendicular distance from the chosen origin to the constant line of motion of the particle. As the particle travels, \(r_\perp\) remains strictly constant.

Step 4: Direction Invariance
The direction of \(\mathbf{r} \times \mathbf{v}\) remains perpendicular to the plane containing the line of motion and the origin, which is fixed in time.

Step 5: Final Conclusion
Both the magnitude and the direction of the angular momentum remain constant throughout the entire motion.

Final Answer: remains constant in both magnitude and direction throughout the motion.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_SYSTEMS_OF_PARTICLES_AND_ROTATIONAL_MOTION_MCQ_Q23 - Translational and rotational effects of a couple

questiontext.text: A pair of equal and opposite parallel forces of magnitude \(F\) acting on a rigid body along separated, distinct lines of action constitutes a couple. Such a couple:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Definition of a Couple
A couple consists of two forces \(\mathbf{F}\) and \(-\mathbf{F}\) having equal magnitudes and opposite directions, separated by a perpendicular distance.

Step 2: Net Force Evaluation
The vector sum of forces is \(\sum \mathbf{F} = \mathbf{F} + (-\mathbf{F}) = \mathbf{0}\). Therefore, the body is in translational equilibrium and experiences no linear acceleration.

Step 3: Net Torque Evaluation
Because the lines of action do not coincide, the torques of the two forces about any point act in the same rotational sense, producing a non-zero net torque \(\boldsymbol{\tau} = \mathbf{r}_{\text{AB}} \times \mathbf{F} \neq \mathbf{0}\).

Step 4: Final Conclusion
A couple produces pure rotation (angular acceleration) without causing any translation.

Final Answer: produces rotational acceleration without producing any translational acceleration.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_SYSTEMS_OF_PARTICLES_AND_ROTATIONAL_MOTION_MCQ_Q24 - Mechanical advantage and principle of moments of a lever

questiontext.text: An ideal light lever in mechanical equilibrium has a load arm of length \(0.4\text{ m}\) and an effort arm of length \(1.6\text{ m}\). What is the mechanical advantage (\(\text{M.A.}\)) of the lever, and what effort force is required to balance a load of \(200\text{ N}\)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data
Load \(F_1 = 200\text{ N}\), load arm \(d_1 = 0.4\text{ m}\), effort arm \(d_2 = 1.6\text{ m}\).

Step 2: Mechanical Advantage Formula
The mechanical advantage of a lever is defined as the ratio of effort arm to load arm:
\[\text{M.A.} = \frac{d_2}{d_1}\]

Step 3: Calculation of Mechanical Advantage
\[\text{M.A.} = \frac{1.6\text{ m}}{0.4\text{ m}} = 4\]

Step 4: Principle of Moments
By rotational equilibrium about the fulcrum: \(\text{Load} \times \text{Load arm} = \text{Effort} \times \text{Effort arm}\), which implies:
\[F_2 = \frac{F_1}{\text{M.A.}} = \frac{200\text{ N}}{4} = 50\text{ N}\]

Step 5: Final Check
\(200\text{ N} \times 0.4\text{ m} = 80\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}\) and \(50\text{ N} \times 1.6\text{ m} = 80\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}\). The moments are balanced.

Final Answer: \(\text{M.A.} = 4\) and Effort \(= 50\text{ N}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_SYSTEMS_OF_PARTICLES_AND_ROTATIONAL_MOTION_MCQ_Q25 - Distinction between center of gravity and center of mass

questiontext.text: The center of gravity (CG) of an extended body coincides with its center of mass (CM) if and only if:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Definition of Center of Gravity
The center of gravity of a body is defined as the point about which the total torque due to gravitational forces on all constituent particles is zero: \(\sum \mathbf{r}_i \times m_i \mathbf{g}_i = \mathbf{0}\).

Step 2: Condition for Coincidence with CM
If the gravitational acceleration \(\mathbf{g}\) is identical (uniform) for all particles of the body, \(\mathbf{g}\) factors out: \(\left(\sum m_i \mathbf{r}_i\right) \times \mathbf{g} = \mathbf{0}\).

Step 3: Relationship to Center of Mass
The condition \(\sum m_i \mathbf{r}_i = \mathbf{0}\) defines the origin as the center of mass. Hence, CG coincides with CM in a uniform gravitational field.

Step 4: Non-uniform Field Case
If the body is so large that \(\mathbf{g}\) varies across its dimensions, the two points diverge because CM depends purely on mass distribution, whereas CG also depends on the local gravitational field variation.

Step 5: Final Conclusion
The center of gravity coincides with the center of mass when the acceleration due to gravity is uniform across all parts of the body.

Final Answer: the acceleration due to gravity is uniform across all parts of the body.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_SYSTEMS_OF_PARTICLES_AND_ROTATIONAL_MOTION_MCQ_Q26 - Moment of inertia of two point masses on a light rod

questiontext.text: A light rigid rod of negligible mass and length \(l\) has two small point masses, each of mass \(M/2\), attached at its two opposite ends. What is the moment of inertia \(I\) of the system about an axis passing through its center of mass perpendicular to the length of the rod?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data
Total mass of system \(= M\). Mass at each end: \(m_1 = M/2\), \(m_2 = M/2\). Length of rod \(= l\).

Step 2: Axis Position and Distances
Since the two masses are equal, the center of mass lies at the midpoint of the rod. The perpendicular distance of each mass from the axis through the center of mass is \(r_1 = r_2 = l/2\).

Step 3: Calculation of Moment of Inertia
Apply the definition \(I = \sum m_i r_i^2\):
\[I = \left(\frac{M}{2}\right)\left(\frac{l}{2}\right)^2 + \left(\frac{M}{2}\right)\left(\frac{l}{2}\right)^2 = \frac{M l^2}{8} + \frac{M l^2}{8} = \frac{M l^2}{4}\]

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The moment of inertia of the system about the perpendicular bisector is \(\frac{1}{4} M l^2\).

Final Answer: \(\frac{1}{4} M l^2\)

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_SYSTEMS_OF_PARTICLES_AND_ROTATIONAL_MOTION_MCQ_Q27 - Radius of gyration of a circular disc about diameter

questiontext.text: The moment of inertia of a uniform circular disc of mass \(M\) and radius \(R\) about any of its diameters is \(I = \frac{1}{4} M R^2\). What is the radius of gyration \(k\) of the disc about this diameter axis?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Formula
Moment of inertia about a diameter: \(I = \frac{1}{4} M R^2\). By definition, the radius of gyration \(k\) is related to total mass \(M\) and moment of inertia \(I\) by \(I = M k^2\).

Step 2: Algebraic Relation
Equating the two expressions for moment of inertia:
\[M k^2 = \frac{1}{4} M R^2\]

Step 3: Solving for k
Dividing both sides by \(M\):
\[k^2 = \frac{R^2}{4} \implies k = \frac{R}{2}\]

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The radius of gyration of the uniform circular disc about its diameter is \(\frac{R}{2}\).

Final Answer: \(\frac{R}{2}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_SYSTEMS_OF_PARTICLES_AND_ROTATIONAL_MOTION_MCQ_Q28 - Moment of inertia and radius of gyration of a thin rod

questiontext.text: A uniform thin rod has mass \(M\) and length \(L\). What is its radius of gyration \(k\) about an axis passing through its midpoint and perpendicular to its length?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Standard Moment of Inertia
From the standard rotational mechanics table, the moment of inertia of a uniform thin rod of length \(L\) and mass \(M\) about an axis perpendicular to the rod at its midpoint is:
\[I = \frac{M L^2}{12}\]

Step 2: Definition of Radius of Gyration
The radius of gyration \(k\) satisfies the identity:
\[I = M k^2\]

Step 3: Calculation of k
Equate the two expressions:
\[M k^2 = \frac{M L^2}{12} \implies k^2 = \frac{L^2}{12} \implies k = \frac{L}{\sqrt{12}}\]

Step 4: Alternative Form
\[\frac{L}{\sqrt{12}} = \frac{L}{2\sqrt{3}}\]

Step 5: Final Conclusion
The radius of gyration of the rod about this central perpendicular axis is \(\frac{L}{\sqrt{12}}\).

Final Answer: \(\frac{L}{\sqrt{12}}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_SYSTEMS_OF_PARTICLES_AND_ROTATIONAL_MOTION_MCQ_Q29 - Angular acceleration from rotational speed increase

questiontext.text: The angular speed of an engine motor wheel is increased uniformly from \(1200\text{ rpm}\) to \(3120\text{ rpm}\) in \(16\text{ seconds}\). What is its angular acceleration \(\alpha\)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data
Initial speed \(N_0 = 1200\text{ rpm}\), final speed \(N = 3120\text{ rpm}\), time interval \(t = 16\text{ s}\).

Step 2: Conversion to Radians per Second
\[\omega_0 = \frac{2\pi N_0}{60} = \frac{2\pi \times 1200}{60} = 40\pi\text{ rad/s}\]
\[\omega = \frac{2\pi N}{60} = \frac{2\pi \times 3120}{60} = 2\pi \times 52 = 104\pi\text{ rad/s}\]

Step 3: Angular Acceleration Formula
For uniform angular acceleration:
\[\alpha = \frac{\omega - \omega_0}{t}\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Calculation
\[\alpha = \frac{104\pi - 40\pi}{16} = \frac{64\pi}{16} = 4\pi\text{ rad/s}^2\]

Step 5: Final Conclusion
The angular acceleration of the motor wheel is \(4\pi\text{ rad/s}^2\).

Final Answer: \(4\pi\text{ rad/s}^2\)

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_SYSTEMS_OF_PARTICLES_AND_ROTATIONAL_MOTION_MCQ_Q30 - Revolutions made during uniform angular acceleration

questiontext.text: A motor wheel accelerates uniformly from \(1200\text{ rpm}\) to \(3120\text{ rpm}\) in \(16\text{ seconds}\). How many complete revolutions does the wheel make during this \(16\text{ s}\) time interval?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Speeds in Radians per Second
\(\omega_0 = 40\pi\text{ rad/s}\), \(\omega = 104\pi\text{ rad/s}\), \(t = 16\text{ s}\), and \(\alpha = 4\pi\text{ rad/s}^2\).

Step 2: Angular Displacement Formula
The total angular displacement in radians is given by:
\[\theta = \omega_0 t + \frac{1}{2}\alpha t^2\]

Step 3: Step-by-Step Calculation
\[\theta = (40\pi \times 16) + \frac{1}{2}(4\pi)(16)^2 = 640\pi + 2\pi(256) = 640\pi + 512\pi = 1152\pi\text{ rad}\]

Step 4: Number of Revolutions
Since one revolution equals \(2\pi\text{ radians}\):
\[N = \frac{\theta}{2\pi} = \frac{1152\pi}{2\pi} = 576\text{ revolutions}\]

Step 5: Alternative Verification
Using average angular speed: \(N = \left(\frac{1200 + 3120}{2 \times 60}\right) \times 16 = \frac{4320}{120} \times 16 = 36 \times 16 = 576\text{ revolutions}\).

Final Answer: \(576\)

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_SYSTEMS_OF_PARTICLES_AND_ROTATIONAL_MOTION_MCQ_Q31 - Power delivered by engine to maintain uniform angular speed

questiontext.text: To maintain a rotor at a uniform angular speed of \(200\text{ rad/s}\), an engine needs to transmit a constant torque of \(180\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}\). Assuming the engine is \(100\%\) efficient, what is the power required by the engine?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data
Torque \(\tau = 180\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}\), angular velocity \(\omega = 200\text{ rad/s}\).

Step 2: Rotational Power Formula
The instantaneous power transmitted in rotational motion about a fixed axis is given by:
\[P = \tau \omega\]

Step 3: Step-by-Step Calculation
Substitute the given values:
\[P = 180\text{ N}\cdot\text{m} \times 200\text{ rad/s} = 36000\text{ W}\]

Step 4: Unit Conversion
Convert watts to kilowatts:
\[P = \frac{36000}{1000}\text{ kW} = 36\text{ kW}\]

Step 5: Final Conclusion
The power required by the engine is \(36\text{ kW}\).

Final Answer: \(36\text{ kW}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_SYSTEMS_OF_PARTICLES_AND_ROTATIONAL_MOTION_MCQ_Q32 - Angular and linear acceleration of pulled hollow cylinder

questiontext.text: A rope of negligible mass is wound round a hollow cylinder of mass \(3\text{ kg}\) and radius \(40\text{ cm}\). The cylinder is free to rotate about its axis of symmetry on frictionless bearings. What are the angular acceleration of the cylinder and the linear acceleration of the rope if the rope is pulled with a steady force of \(30\text{ N}\) without slipping?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data
Mass \(M = 3\text{ kg}\), radius \(R = 40\text{ cm} = 0.4\text{ m}\), applied force \(F = 30\text{ N}\).

Step 2: Moment of Inertia of Hollow Cylinder
For a thin-walled hollow cylinder about its central axis:
\[I = M R^2 = 3\text{ kg} \times (0.4\text{ m})^2 = 3 \times 0.16 = 0.48\text{ kg}\cdot\text{m}^2\]

Step 3: Applied Torque
\[\tau = F R = 30\text{ N} \times 0.4\text{ m} = 12\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}\]

Step 4: Angular Acceleration
Using Newton's second law for rotation, \(\tau = I\alpha\):
\[\alpha = \frac{\tau}{I} = \frac{12\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}}{0.48\text{ kg}\cdot\text{m}^2} = 25\text{ rad/s}^2\]

Step 5: Linear Acceleration of Rope
Since the rope unrolls tangentially without slipping:
\[a = \alpha R = 25\text{ rad/s}^2 \times 0.4\text{ m} = 10\text{ m/s}^2\]

Final Answer: \(\alpha = 25\text{ rad/s}^2\) and \(a = 10\text{ m/s}^2\)

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_SYSTEMS_OF_PARTICLES_AND_ROTATIONAL_MOTION_MCQ_Q33 - Kinetic energy and angular momentum of rotating solid cylinder

questiontext.text: A solid cylinder of mass \(20\text{ kg}\) and radius \(0.25\text{ m}\) rotates about its standard axis of symmetry with an angular speed of \(100\text{ rad/s}\). What are the kinetic energy associated with the rotation of the cylinder and the magnitude of its angular momentum about its axis?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data
Mass \(M = 20\text{ kg}\), radius \(R = 0.25\text{ m}\), angular speed \(\omega = 100\text{ rad/s}\).

Step 2: Moment of Inertia of Solid Cylinder
For a solid cylinder about its geometric axis:
\[I = \frac{1}{2} M R^2 = \frac{1}{2}(20)(0.25)^2 = 10 \times 0.0625 = 0.625\text{ kg}\cdot\text{m}^2\]

Step 3: Rotational Kinetic Energy
\[K = \frac{1}{2} I \omega^2 = \frac{1}{2}(0.625)(100)^2 = 0.3125 \times 10000 = 3125\text{ J}\]

Step 4: Magnitude of Angular Momentum
\[L = I \omega = 0.625\text{ kg}\cdot\text{m}^2 \times 100\text{ rad/s} = 62.5\text{ J}\cdot\text{s}\text{ (or kg}\cdot\text{m}^2/\text{s)}\]

Step 5: Relation Check
\[K = \frac{L^2}{2I} = \frac{(62.5)^2}{2(0.625)} = \frac{3906.25}{1.25} = 3125\text{ J}\]

Final Answer: \(K = 3125\text{ J}\) and \(L = 62.5\text{ J}\cdot\text{s}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_SYSTEMS_OF_PARTICLES_AND_ROTATIONAL_MOTION_MCQ_Q34 - Angular speed of child on rotating turntable

questiontext.text: A child stands at the center of a turntable with arms outstretched, rotating with an initial angular speed of \(40\text{ rev/min}\) on frictionless bearings. How much is the angular speed of the child if they fold their arms back, thereby reducing their moment of inertia to \(\frac{2}{5}\) times the initial value?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Initial angular speed \(\omega_1 = 40\text{ rev/min}\). Initial moment of inertia \(I_1\). Final moment of inertia \(I_2 = \frac{2}{5} I_1\). Net external torque \(\tau_{\text{ext}} = 0\).

Step 2: Governing Principle
Since external torque about the vertical rotation axis is zero, the angular momentum of the system is strictly conserved:
\[I_1 \omega_1 = I_2 \omega_2\]

Step 3: Calculation of Final Angular Speed
\[\omega_2 = \frac{I_1}{I_2} \omega_1 = \frac{I_1}{\frac{2}{5} I_1} \times 40 = \frac{5}{2} \times 40 = 100\text{ rev/min}\]

Step 4: Check and Plausibility
Reducing the moment of inertia by folding arms redistributes mass closer to the rotation axis, causing angular speed to increase proportionally.

Final Answer: \(100\text{ rev/min}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_SYSTEMS_OF_PARTICLES_AND_ROTATIONAL_MOTION_MCQ_Q35 - Kinetic energy increase due to internal muscular work

questiontext.text: A child rotating freely on a frictionless turntable folds their arms, reducing their moment of inertia to \(\frac{2}{5}\) of its initial value. What is the ratio of the new rotational kinetic energy to the initial rotational kinetic energy, and what is the physical reason for this change?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Conditions
Moment of inertia ratio: \(I_2 = \frac{2}{5} I_1\). Angular momentum \(L\) is conserved: \(L_1 = L_2 = L\).

Step 2: Kinetic Energy Expression in Terms of Angular Momentum
Rotational kinetic energy can be expressed as:
\[K = \frac{1}{2} I \omega^2 = \frac{L^2}{2I}\]

Step 3: Ratio of Kinetic Energies
\[\frac{K_2}{K_1} = \frac{L^2 / (2 I_2)}{L^2 / (2 I_1)} = \frac{I_1}{I_2} = \frac{I_1}{\frac{2}{5} I_1} = \frac{5}{2} = 2.5\]

Step 4: Physical Explanation of Energy Source
Rotational kinetic energy increases by a factor of \(2.5\). This extra mechanical energy comes from the internal muscular work done by the child to pull their arms inwards against the outward centrifugal inertial force.

Step 5: Final Conclusion
The ratio of new to initial rotational kinetic energy is \(2.5\), and the increase is supplied by internal muscular work done by the child.

Final Answer: The ratio is \(2.5\), and the increase is due to internal muscular work done by the child.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_SYSTEMS_OF_PARTICLES_AND_ROTATIONAL_MOTION_MCQ_Q36 - Work done and kinetic energy of cord unwound from flywheel

questiontext.text: A cord of negligible mass is wound round the rim of a flywheel of mass \(20\text{ kg}\) and radius \(20\text{ cm}\) mounted on a frictionless horizontal axle. A steady pulling force of \(25\text{ N}\) is applied to the cord. Assuming the wheel starts from rest, what is the kinetic energy gained by the wheel when \(2\text{ m}\) of the cord has been unwound?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data
Mass \(M = 20\text{ kg}\), radius \(R = 20\text{ cm} = 0.20\text{ m}\), force \(F = 25\text{ N}\), length of unwound cord \(s = 2\text{ m}\). Initial angular velocity \(\omega_0 = 0\).

Step 2: Work-Energy Theorem for Rotation
By the work-energy theorem, the change in rotational kinetic energy of the rigid body equals the work done by the torque:
\[\Delta K = W = \tau \theta\]

Step 3: Calculating Torque and Angular Displacement
\[\tau = F R = 25\text{ N} \times 0.20\text{ m} = 5.0\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}\]
\[\theta = \frac{s}{R} = \frac{2\text{ m}}{0.20\text{ m}} = 10\text{ rad}\]

Step 4: Work Done Calculation
\[W = \tau \theta = 5.0\text{ N}\cdot\text{m} \times 10\text{ rad} = 50\text{ J}\]
Directly from the force: \(W = F s = 25\text{ N} \times 2\text{ m} = 50\text{ J}\).

Step 5: Final Check
Since the wheel starts from rest and bearing friction is absent, the kinetic energy gained by the wheel is exactly equal to the work done by the pulling force, which is \(50\text{ J}\).

Final Answer: \(50\text{ J}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_SYSTEMS_OF_PARTICLES_AND_ROTATIONAL_MOTION_MCQ_Q37 - Shift of center of mass of disc with circular hole

questiontext.text: From a uniform circular disc of radius \(R\) centered at the origin, a circular hole of radius \(R/2\) is cut out. The center of the cutout hole is situated at \((R/2, 0)\). What are the coordinates of the center of mass of the remaining flat body?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Principle of Negative Mass
Let the uniform original disc have surface mass density \(\sigma\). The original disc had radius \(R\), area \(A_1 = \pi R^2\), and center of mass at \((0, 0)\). The removed circular portion has radius \(R/2\), area \(A_2 = \pi (R/2)^2 = \frac{\pi R^2}{4}\), and center of mass at \((R/2, 0)\).

Step 2: Center of Mass Formula for Subtracted Mass
The center of mass coordinate along the \(x\)-axis is given by:
\[X = \frac{A_1 x_1 - A_2 x_2}{A_1 - A_2}\]

Step 3: Step-by-Step Substitution
\[X = \frac{(\pi R^2)(0) - \left(\frac{\pi R^2}{4}\right)\left(\frac{R}{2}\right)}{\pi R^2 - \frac{\pi R^2}{4}} = \frac{-\frac{\pi R^3}{8}}{\frac{3\pi R^2}{4}}\]

Step 4: Algebraic Simplification
\[X = -\frac{R}{8} \times \frac{4}{3} = -\frac{R}{6}\]
Since the figure is symmetric with respect to the \(x\)-axis, \(Y = 0\).

Step 5: Final Check
Removing mass from the positive \(x\)-side shifts the center of mass to the opposite (negative \(x\)) side by \(R/6\). The coordinates are \(\left(-\frac{R}{6}, 0\right)\).

Final Answer: \(\left(-\frac{R}{6}, 0\right)\)

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_SYSTEMS_OF_PARTICLES_AND_ROTATIONAL_MOTION_MCQ_Q38 - Mass of a balanced metre stick with coins

questiontext.text: A uniform metre stick is balanced on a knife edge at its center of gravity at the \(50.0\text{ cm}\) mark. When two identical coins, each of mass \(5.0\text{ g}\), are placed one on top of the other at the \(12.0\text{ cm}\) mark, the stick is found to be balanced horizontally when the knife edge is shifted to the \(45.0\text{ cm}\) mark. What is the mass of the metre stick?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Positions
Mass of the two coins: \(m = 2 \times 5.0\text{ g} = 10.0\text{ g}\). Position of coins: \(x_{\text{coins}} = 12.0\text{ cm}\). New fulcrum position: \(x_{\text{f}} = 45.0\text{ cm}\). Center of gravity of uniform stick: \(x_{\text{CG}} = 50.0\text{ cm}\).

Step 2: Lever Arm Calculations
Distance of coins from fulcrum: \(d_1 = 45.0 - 12.0 = 33.0\text{ cm}\).
Distance of stick's center of gravity from fulcrum: \(d_2 = 50.0 - 45.0 = 5.0\text{ cm}\).

Step 3: Rotational Equilibrium Principle
Taking torques about the knife edge fulcrum:
\[m \cdot g \cdot d_1 = M_{\text{stick}} \cdot g \cdot d_2\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Calculation
Cancel \(g\) from both sides:
\[10.0\text{ g} \times 33.0\text{ cm} = M_{\text{stick}} \times 5.0\text{ cm}\]
\[M_{\text{stick}} = \frac{330.0}{5.0}\text{ g} = 66.0\text{ g}\]

Step 5: Final Check
Torques balance: \(10\text{ g} \times 33\text{ cm} = 330\text{ g}\cdot\text{cm}\) and \(66\text{ g} \times 5\text{ cm} = 330\text{ g}\cdot\text{cm}\).

Final Answer: \(66\text{ g}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_SYSTEMS_OF_PARTICLES_AND_ROTATIONAL_MOTION_MCQ_Q39 - Reactions at knife edges supporting loaded metal bar

questiontext.text: A homogeneous metal bar \(70\text{ cm}\) long and of mass \(4.00\text{ kg}\) is supported horizontally on two knife-edges placed \(10\text{ cm}\) from each end. A \(6.00\text{ kg}\) load is suspended at \(30\text{ cm}\) from the left end. Taking \(g = 9.8\text{ m/s}^2\), what are the normal reactions \(R_1\) and \(R_2\) at the left and right knife-edges respectively?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Positions and Forces
Bar length \(AB = 70\text{ cm}\). Center of gravity \(G\) is at \(35\text{ cm}\) from \(A\). Left knife-edge \(K_1\) at \(10\text{ cm}\) from \(A\); right knife-edge \(K_2\) at \(60\text{ cm}\) from \(A\). Load \(W_1 = 6.00g\text{ N}\) suspended at \(P\) (\(30\text{ cm}\) from \(A\)). Bar weight \(W = 4.00g\text{ N}\) at \(G\).

Step 2: Translational Equilibrium
Equating upward reactions to total downward weight:
\[R_1 + R_2 = W_1 + W = (6.00 + 4.00)g = 10.00g = 98.00\text{ N}\]

Step 3: Distances from Center of Gravity G
\[K_1 G = 35 - 10 = 25\text{ cm} = 0.25\text{ m}\]
\[K_2 G = 60 - 35 = 25\text{ cm} = 0.25\text{ m}\]
\[P G = 35 - 30 = 5\text{ cm} = 0.05\text{ m}\]

Step 4: Rotational Equilibrium about G
Taking counter-clockwise torques as positive and clockwise as negative:
\[-R_1(K_1 G) + W_1(P G) + R_2(K_2 G) = 0\]
\[-0.25 R_1 + 0.05(6.00g) + 0.25 R_2 = 0 \implies 0.25(R_1 - R_2) = 0.30g\]
\[R_1 - R_2 = \frac{0.30}{0.25}g = 1.20g = 1.20 \times 9.8 = 11.76\text{ N}\]

Step 5: Solving Simultaneous Equations
\[R_1 = \frac{98.00 + 11.76}{2} = 54.88\text{ N} \approx 55\text{ N}\]
\[R_2 = \frac{98.00 - 11.76}{2} = 43.12\text{ N} \approx 43\text{ N}\]

Final Answer: \(R_1 \approx 55\text{ N}\) and \(R_2 \approx 43\text{ N}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_SYSTEMS_OF_PARTICLES_AND_ROTATIONAL_MOTION_MCQ_Q40 - Reaction forces on a ladder leaning against frictionless wall

questiontext.text: A \(3\text{ m}\) long uniform ladder of mass \(20\text{ kg}\) leans against a frictionless vertical wall, with its foot resting on the floor \(1\text{ m}\) from the base of the wall. Taking \(g = 9.8\text{ m/s}^2\), what is the normal reaction force exerted by the wall on the upper end of the ladder?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Geometry and Forces
Ladder \(AB = 3\text{ m}\). Distance of foot from wall \(AC = 1\text{ m}\). By Pythagoras theorem, the vertical height reached by the ladder on the wall is:
\[BC = \sqrt{AB^2 - AC^2} = \sqrt{3^2 - 1^2} = \sqrt{8} = 2\sqrt{2}\text{ m}\]

Step 2: Center of Gravity and Weight
The ladder is uniform, so its weight acts at the midpoint \(D\):
\[W = mg = 20 \times 9.8 = 196.0\text{ N}\]
The horizontal distance from the foot \(A\) to the vertical line of action of \(W\) is \(AE = \frac{1}{2} AC = 0.5\text{ m}\).

Step 3: Reaction of Frictionless Wall
Because the wall is frictionless, its reaction force \(F_1\) is purely horizontal (perpendicular to the wall).

Step 4: Rotational Equilibrium about Foot A
Taking torques about foot \(A\) eliminates the floor reaction forces:
\[F_1(BC) - W(AE) = 0\]
\[F_1 (2\sqrt{2}\text{ m}) - (196.0\text{ N})(0.5\text{ m}) = 0\]
\[F_1 = \frac{98.0}{2\sqrt{2}} = \frac{49.0}{\sqrt{2}} = \frac{49.0}{1.4142} \approx 34.6\text{ N}\]

Step 5: Final Check
Translational equilibrium in the horizontal direction gives the frictional force at the floor as \(F = F_1 = 34.6\text{ N}\), which is physically plausible.

Final Answer: \(34.6\text{ N}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_SYSTEMS_OF_PARTICLES_AND_ROTATIONAL_MOTION_MCQ_Q41 - Center of gravity of non-uniform bar suspended by strings

questiontext.text: A non-uniform bar of weight \(W\) and length \(2\text{ m}\) is suspended horizontally at rest by two light strings attached at its ends. The left string makes an angle of \(36.9^\circ\) with the vertical, and the right string makes an angle of \(53.1^\circ\) with the vertical (with \(\sin 36.9^\circ = \cos 53.1^\circ = 0.6\) and \(\cos 36.9^\circ = \sin 53.1^\circ = 0.8\)). What is the distance \(d\) of the center of gravity of the bar from its left end?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Conditions and Equilibrium Equations
Bar length \(L = 2\text{ m}\). Let tensions in the left and right strings be \(T_1\) and \(T_2\).
Angles with the vertical: \(\theta_1 = 36.9^\circ\), \(\theta_2 = 53.1^\circ\).

Step 2: Horizontal Translational Equilibrium
\[T_1 \sin 36.9^\circ = T_2 \sin 53.1^\circ \implies T_1(0.6) = T_2(0.8) \implies T_2 = \frac{3}{4} T_1\]

Step 3: Vertical Translational Equilibrium
\[T_1 \cos 36.9^\circ + T_2 \cos 53.1^\circ = W\]
Substitute \(T_2 = \frac{3}{4} T_1\):
\[T_1(0.8) + \left(\frac{3}{4} T_1\right)(0.6) = 0.8 T_1 + 0.45 T_1 = 1.25 T_1 = W \implies T_1 = \frac{W}{1.25} = 0.8 W\]
\[T_2 = \frac{3}{4}(0.8 W) = 0.6 W\]

Step 4: Rotational Equilibrium about Left End
Taking torques about the left end:
\[W \cdot d = (T_2 \cos 53.1^\circ) \cdot L\]
Substitute \(T_2 = 0.6 W\), \(\cos 53.1^\circ = 0.6\), and \(L = 2\text{ m}\):
\[W \cdot d = (0.6 W)(0.6)(2\text{ m}) = 0.72 W\text{ m} \implies d = 0.72\text{ m}\]

Step 5: Verification
The distance \(d = 0.72\text{ m}\) is less than half the length (\(1.0\text{ m}\)), consistent with the left string carrying more tension and having a steeper vertical angle.

Final Answer: \(0.72\text{ m}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_SYSTEMS_OF_PARTICLES_AND_ROTATIONAL_MOTION_MCQ_Q42 - Forces exerted by ground on front and back wheels of a car

questiontext.text: A car weighs \(1800\text{ kg}\). The distance between its front and back axles is \(1.80\text{ m}\). Its center of gravity is \(1.05\text{ m}\) behind the front axle on level ground. Taking \(g = 9.8\text{ m/s}^2\), what are the vertical normal forces exerted by the ground on each front wheel and on each back wheel?

Step 1: Given Data
Mass \(M = 1800\text{ kg}\). Total weight \(W = 1800 \times 9.8 = 17640\text{ N}\). Wheelbase \(L = 1.80\text{ m}\). Distance of CG from front axle \(d_f = 1.05\text{ m}\). Distance of CG from back axle \(d_b = 1.80 - 1.05 = 0.75\text{ m}\).

Step 2: Total Axle Reactions
Let total normal force on the front axle be \(R_f\) and on the back axle be \(R_b\). For translational equilibrium: \(R_f + R_b = W = 17640\text{ N}\).

Step 3: Torque Equilibrium about Back Axle
Taking torques about the back axle line:
\[R_f \times 1.80\text{ m} - W \times 0.75\text{ m} = 0\]
\[R_f = \frac{0.75}{1.80} \times 17640 = \frac{5}{12} \times 17640 = 7350\text{ N}\]

Step 4: Torque Equilibrium about Front Axle

Each axle has two wheels sharing the load equally:
Force on each front wheel \(= \frac{7350}{2} = 3675\text{ N}\).
Force on each back wheel \(= \frac{10290}{2} = 5145\text{ N}\).

Final Answer: \(3675\text{ N}\) on each front wheel and \(5145\text{ N}\) on each back wheel

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_SYSTEMS_OF_PARTICLES_AND_ROTATIONAL_MOTION_MCQ_Q43 - Angular speed comparison of hollow cylinder vs solid sphere

questiontext.text: Torques of equal magnitude are applied from rest to a hollow cylinder and a solid sphere, both having identical mass \(M\) and radius \(R\). The cylinder rotates about its standard axis of symmetry, and the sphere rotates about an axis passing through its center. Which of the two will acquire a greater angular speed after a given time \(t\)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Moments of Inertia
Hollow cylinder: \(I_c = M R^2\). Solid sphere: \(I_s = \frac{2}{5} M R^2 = 0.4 M R^2\). Both bodies have identical mass \(M\) and radius \(R\).

Step 2: Angular Acceleration Expression
The angular acceleration produced by a torque \(\tau\) is \(\alpha = \frac{\tau}{I}\).
For the cylinder: \(\alpha_c = \frac{\tau}{M R^2}\).
For the sphere: \(\alpha_s = \frac{\tau}{\frac{2}{5} M R^2} = 2.5 \frac{\tau}{M R^2}\).

Step 3: Comparison of Angular Accelerations
Since \(I_s < I_c\), the angular acceleration of the solid sphere is \(2.5\) times greater than that of the hollow cylinder: \(\alpha_s = 2.5 \alpha_c\).

Step 4: Angular Speed after Time t
Starting from rest, the angular speed achieved after time \(t\) is \(\omega = \alpha t\). Therefore, \(\omega_s = 2.5 \omega_c\).

Step 5: Final Conclusion
The solid sphere acquires a greater angular speed because its mass is concentrated closer to the rotation axis, resulting in a smaller moment of inertia.

Final Answer: The solid sphere, because its mass is distributed closer to the axis, giving it a smaller moment of inertia and higher angular acceleration.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_SYSTEMS_OF_PARTICLES_AND_ROTATIONAL_MOTION_MCQ_Q44 - Average angular velocity of oxygen molecule

questiontext.text: An oxygen molecule has a mass of \(5.30 \times 10^{-26}\text{ kg}\) and a moment of inertia of \(1.94 \times 10^{-40}\text{ kg}\cdot\text{m}^2\) about an axis through its center perpendicular to the internuclear axis. If the mean translational speed of the molecule is \(500\text{ m/s}\) and its rotational kinetic energy is \(\frac{2}{3}\) of its translational kinetic energy, what is the average angular velocity \(\omega\) of the molecule?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data
Mass \(m = 5.30 \times 10^{-26}\text{ kg}\), \(I = 1.94 \times 10^{-40}\text{ kg}\cdot\text{m}^2\), \(v = 500\text{ m/s}\).

Step 2: Translational Kinetic Energy Calculation
\[K_{\text{trans}} = \frac{1}{2} m v^2 = \frac{1}{2}(5.30 \times 10^{-26})(500)^2 = \frac{1}{2}(5.30 \times 10^{-26})(2.5 \times 10^5) = 6.625 \times 10^{-21}\text{ J}\]

Step 3: Rotational Kinetic Energy
\[K_{\text{rot}} = \frac{2}{3} K_{\text{trans}} = \frac{2}{3}(6.625 \times 10^{-21}) = 4.4167 \times 10^{-21}\text{ J}\]

Step 4: Angular Velocity Calculation
Using \(K_{\text{rot}} = \frac{1}{2} I \omega^2\):
\[\omega^2 = \frac{2 K_{\text{rot}}}{I} = \frac{2(4.4167 \times 10^{-21})}{1.94 \times 10^{-40}} = \frac{8.8333 \times 10^{-21}}{1.94 \times 10^{-40}} \approx 4.553 \times 10^{19}\text{ rad}^2/\text{s}^2\]

Step 5: Square Root Evaluation
\[\omega = \sqrt{45.53 \times 10^{18}} \approx 6.75 \times 10^{12}\text{ rad/s}\]

Final Answer: \(6.75 \times 10^{12}\text{ rad/s}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_SYSTEMS_OF_PARTICLES_AND_ROTATIONAL_MOTION_MCQ_Q45 - Angular momentum of two particles moving along parallel lines

questiontext.text: Two particles, each of mass \(m\), travel in opposite directions with the same speed \(v\) along parallel lines separated by a perpendicular distance \(d\). What can be asserted regarding the total angular momentum \(\mathbf{L}\) of this two-particle system?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: System Definition
Consider particle 1 moving with velocity \(\mathbf{v}_1 = v\hat{\mathbf{i}}\) along the line \(y = d_1\), and particle 2 moving with velocity \(\mathbf{v}_2 = -v\hat{\mathbf{i}}\) along the line \(y = d_2\), where the perpendicular separation is \(|d_1 - d_2| = d\).

Step 2: Angular Momentum Calculation
Let the position vectors of the particles from an arbitrary origin \(O\) be \(\mathbf{r}_1\) and \(\mathbf{r}_2\). The total angular momentum is:
\[\mathbf{L} = \mathbf{r}_1 \times (m\mathbf{v}_1) + \mathbf{r}_2 \times (m\mathbf{v}_2) = m [\mathbf{r}_1 \times \mathbf{v} - \mathbf{r}_2 \times \mathbf{v}] = m (\mathbf{r}_1 - \mathbf{r}_2) \times \mathbf{v}\]

Step 3: Independence of Origin
The vector difference \(\mathbf{r}_1 - \mathbf{r}_2\) represents the relative position vector between the two particles, which is completely independent of the selection of origin \(O\).

Step 4: Magnitude Calculation
The magnitude of the cross product is \(|(\mathbf{r}_1 - \mathbf{r}_2) \times \mathbf{v}| = |\mathbf{r}_1 - \mathbf{r}_2| v \sin\phi = v d\), where \(d\) is the perpendicular distance between the lines of motion. Hence, \(|\mathbf{L}| = mvd\).

Step 5: Final Conclusion
The total angular momentum has magnitude \(mvd\) and is completely independent of the selection of origin.

Final Answer: has magnitude \(mvd\) and is independent of the selection of origin.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_SYSTEMS_OF_PARTICLES_AND_ROTATIONAL_MOTION_MCQ_Q46 - Geometric interpretations of cross product and scalar triple product

questiontext.text: For three non-coplanar vectors \(\mathbf{a}\), \(\mathbf{b}\), and \(\mathbf{c}\), which of the following expressions correctly states their geometric interpretations?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Cross Product and Triangle Area
The magnitude of the vector cross product \(|\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b}| = ab\sin\theta\) equals the area of the parallelogram formed by \(\mathbf{a}\) and \(\mathbf{b}\). The triangle formed by vectors \(\mathbf{a}\) and \(\mathbf{b}\) occupies exactly half this area: \(\text{Area} = \frac{1}{2}|\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b}|\).

Step 2: Scalar Triple Product and Parallelepiped Volume
The scalar triple product is defined as \(\mathbf{a} \cdot (\mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{c})\). Here \(\mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{c}\) represents a vector whose magnitude is the base area of the parallelepiped and whose direction is perpendicular to the base.

Step 3: Volume Calculation
The dot product with \(\mathbf{a}\) multiplies the base area by the perpendicular height \(a\cos\phi\), yielding the volume of the parallelepiped: \(V = |\mathbf{a} \cdot (\mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{c})|\).

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The area of the triangle is \(\frac{1}{2}|\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b}|\), and the volume of the parallelepiped is \(|\mathbf{a} \cdot (\mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{c})|\).

Final Answer: The area of the triangle formed by \(\mathbf{a}\) and \(\mathbf{b}\) is \(\frac{1}{2}|\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b}|\), and the volume of the parallelepiped formed by \(\mathbf{a}\), \(\mathbf{b}\), and \(\mathbf{c}\) is \(|\mathbf{a} \cdot (\mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{c})|\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_SYSTEMS_OF_PARTICLES_AND_ROTATIONAL_MOTION_MCQ_Q47 - Collinearity of angular momentum and angular velocity

questiontext.text: For a rigid body rotating about a fixed axis with angular velocity \(\boldsymbol{\omega}\), the total angular momentum \(\mathbf{L}\) of the body is strictly parallel to \(\boldsymbol{\omega}\) if and only if:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: General Angular Momentum of Rotating Body
For a rotating rigid body, the total angular momentum is decomposed into components parallel and perpendicular to the rotation axis: \(\mathbf{L} = \mathbf{L}_z + \mathbf{L}_\perp\), where \(\mathbf{L}_z = I \boldsymbol{\omega}\).

Step 2: Analysis of Perpendicular Component
The perpendicular component is \(\mathbf{L}_\perp = \sum \mathbf{OC}_i \times m_i \mathbf{v}_i\). In general, this perpendicular component does not vanish.

Step 3: Role of Symmetry
When the axis of rotation is an axis of symmetry of the body, for every mass element having velocity \(\mathbf{v}_i\), there is a diametrically opposite element of equal mass having velocity \(-\mathbf{v}_i\). Their contributions to \(\mathbf{L}_\perp\) cancel exactly, ensuring \(\mathbf{L}_\perp = \mathbf{0}\).

Step 4: Final Conclusion
For asymmetric bodies, \(\mathbf{L}\) and \(\boldsymbol{\omega}\) are not parallel. They are strictly parallel if and only if the axis of rotation is an axis of symmetry of the body.

Final Answer: the axis of rotation is an axis of symmetry of the body.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_SYSTEMS_OF_PARTICLES_AND_ROTATIONAL_MOTION_MCQ_Q48 - Precession of a rotating bicycle rim

questiontext.text: A bicycle rim is set in fast rotation in a vertical plane about its horizontal axle. When one end of the axle is supported by a vertical string and the other end is released, the axle precesses horizontally rather than immediately toppling downward. What is the fundamental physical reason for this behavior?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Initial Angular Momentum Vector
When the rim rotates rapidly in a vertical plane, its spin angular momentum vector \(\mathbf{L}\) is directed horizontally along its axle.

Step 2: External Torque Vector
When one end of the horizontal axle is supported by the string, the unsupported weight \(Mg\) acting downwards at the center of gravity exerts an external torque \(\boldsymbol{\tau} = \mathbf{r} \times M\mathbf{g}\). The direction of this torque is horizontal and perpendicular to the axle (and thus perpendicular to \(\mathbf{L}\)).

Step 3: Rate of Change of Angular Momentum
According to the rotational second law, \(\frac{\mathrm{d}\mathbf{L}}{\mathrm{d}t} = \boldsymbol{\tau}\). Since \(\boldsymbol{\tau}\) is perpendicular to \(\mathbf{L}\), the change \(\mathrm{d}\mathbf{L}\) in any small time \(\mathrm{d}t\) is perpendicular to \(\mathbf{L}\).

Step 4: Gyroscopic Precession
A force perpendicular to linear momentum alters its direction without changing speed, producing circular motion. Analogously, a torque perpendicular to angular momentum alters the direction of \(\mathbf{L}\) without altering its magnitude, forcing the axle to precess in a horizontal circle about the supporting string.

Step 5: Final Conclusion
The horizontal precession occurs because the gravitational torque is perpendicular to the horizontal spin angular momentum, changing its direction without altering its magnitude.

Final Answer: the downward torque due to gravity is perpendicular to the horizontal angular momentum, changing its direction without changing its magnitude.
